messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Entrapment: Having no options
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Valentina Reyes is a 27-year-old Salvadoran American woman who works as an HVAC technician for a commercial contracting company in the Houston area. She came to the intake appointment alone, dressed in her work uniform, and spoke carefully, choosing words with a deliberateness that suggested she had rehearsed what she was willing to say. She has never been in therapy before. She described herself, before everything happened, as someone who was "good at handling things."

Approximately fourteen months ago, Valentina was abducted by two women connected to a debt dispute involving a family member. She was held for several days in a residential property, restrained, and subjected to repeated physical violence by her captors — both of whom were female. She described moments when the door to the room was locked from the outside and she understood, with complete clarity, that there was nothing she could do. No exit. No choice. No way to make it stop. She was eventually released and found her way to a hospital, where her injuries were treated. She did not report the incident to police. She told no one in her family what had happened to her. She returned to work within two weeks.

In the months that followed, Valentina's world quietly contracted. The memory of what happened does not come to her as a coherent story she can tell — it arrives in fragments that feel, she has said, like they happened to a different person, someone she watches from a distance rather than remembers from the inside. And yet when those fragments surface, they bring with them a wave of emotion so total that she has to put down whatever she is holding, leave the room, and wait for it to pass. What accompanies those moments, more than fear, is shame — a shame she cannot fully explain but cannot escape, a feeling that something about what was done to her reflects something about who she is.

She has come to believe, in a way that feels less like a thought and more like a fact, that she cannot know who will harm her. This is not paranoia she can talk herself out of. It sits beneath her reasoning like a foundation. Women, in particular, have become a source of vigilance she cannot suppress. When her job requires her to work alone in a building with a female facilities manager or a female colleague, something in her body goes on alert. She has begun scheduling her work orders to minimize those situations, sometimes telling her supervisor she needs to revisit a site solo for "equipment checks" that do not strictly require a second visit. Her supervisor has noticed the pattern. A performance review last month flagged her as "inconsistent in her team coordination," and she did not explain why.

At home, her evenings follow a fixed sequence she did not consciously design. She checks the locks on her front door and windows before bed, and again if she wakes in the night — which she does, regularly, surfacing from sleep already scanning the room for something she cannot name. She startles at sounds she would once have ignored: a cabinet closing in the next apartment, a car door in the parking lot. She has told herself that this alertness is reasonable, that it would be foolish not to stay ready, and yet some part of her knows it is costing her something she is not getting back.

What troubles Valentina most, perhaps, is a quieter damage she is less able to articulate. She has come to believe she is not the same person she was before, that whatever was broken during those days has not healed but calcified. She doubts her own judgment in ways she never did before — not just about other people, but about herself, whether she will respond correctly, whether she can be trusted to do the right thing in a moment that matters. She has not been in a relationship since the assault and does not expect to be.

She sought help now because the job review frightened her. Not because she feared losing her position, but because she realized, reading her supervisor's words, that what had happened to her was becoming visible — that it was changing the shape of her life in ways other people could see, even if they did not know what they were looking at.
